notes: Dark formal column that broadens with age; tie in against snow; all parts except the red aril toxic.
Very hardy upright yew, the standard formal hedge at 2–3 per m; regrows from old wood; toxic.
Native heath and pasture juniper; slow; berries flavour gin and sauerkraut; needs sun and lean soil.
Dense steel-blue dwarf for rock gardens, gravel and pots; slow and almost maintenance-free.

origin: Mountains of S & C Europe to C Asia
notes: Tough spreading juniper for sunny slopes and lime; very poisonous; alternate host of pear rust.
Pencil-thin blue-grey column, a hardy stand-in for Italian cypress; tie in against snow.
Silver-blue carpet tinged purple in winter; for sunny banks, rock gardens and wall tops.
Iconic Tuscan and Provençal column; needs sun and sharp drainage; hardy to about −15 °C.
Umbrella pine with edible pine nuts; flat crown develops with age; hardy to about −12 °C.
Tough dark-needled pine for wind, lime and drought; good windbreak; too big for small plots.
Slow, dense Alpine pine (Zirbe) with soft blue-green needles; edible seeds; prefers cool sites.
Dense dwarf globe for rock gardens and pots; pinch new candles by half in May to keep it tight.
Native mountain fir, shade-tolerant when young; needs humid air; dislikes pollution and drought.
Glossy dark Christmas-tree fir in even tiers with soft needles; reaches 20 m+, so plan the room.
Compact fir with violet-blue upright cones even when young; needles silver beneath.
Native spruce; fast but shallow-rooted and drought-stressed in lowlands; too big for most gardens.
Flat-topped, nest-shaped dwarf spruce; slow and tidy for rock gardens, heather beds and edges.
Slender spire with silver-backed needles; tolerates lime and city air; suits smaller plots.
Deciduous conifer: fresh green in spring, gold in autumn; fast and casts only light shade.
Majestic silver-blue specimen that spreads wide with age; needs a big lawn; drought-tolerant.
Flat-tiered giant of English landscape parks; conical when young; only for very large gardens.
Fast hedging thuja (30–40 cm/yr), plant 60 cm apart; clip twice a year; no regrowth from bare wood.
Dense dwarf globe for edging, rock gardens and pots; bronze-tinged in winter.
Glossy, fruity-scented foliage; fast hedge at 1.5 per m; takes more shade than other thujas.
Narrow blue-grey column for formal accents or screens; never cut back into bare brown wood.
Feathery conifer carpet that copes with shade and turns coppery-bronze in winter; very hardy.
Fast deciduous 'living fossil' with feathery needles and russet autumn colour; loves moist soil.
Deciduous conifer for pond and lake edges; forms woody 'knees' in wet soil; rusty autumn colour.
Landmark giant with soft red bark; up to 1 m a year when young; only for parks and estates.
Classic dwarf parterre edging, 5–6 per m; watch for box moth and box blight; toxic.

origin: W, C & S Europe, N Africa
notes: Red berries only on females with a male nearby; slow, dense hedge or topiary; berries toxic.
Box-free alternative for low hedges and balls, 3–4 per m; needs lime-free, evenly moist soil.
Native semi-evergreen hedge, 3 per m; 'Atrovirens' holds its leaves best; black berries toxic.
Classic glossy town hedge, 3 per m; clip 2–3 times a year; drops leaves in hard winters.
Fast tiny-leaved box substitute for low hedges and shapes; needs clipping 2–3 times a year.
Glossy evergreen with bright red young shoots, best after clipping; hedge 2 per m; to about −15 °C.
Glossy, salt-tolerant evergreen for seaside hedges and clipped shapes; prone to mildew in shade.
Apple-green, salt-proof coastal hedge at 2 per m; may be damaged inland below about −10 °C.
Compact glossy coastal hedge with pink-and-white flowers all summer; trim after flowering.
Tough silvery-green screen; tiny hidden flowers in Oct–Nov are intensely sweet-scented.
Slow, dense evergreen with jasmine-scented white flowers in April; clips into hedges or balls.
Purple leaves turning scarlet in autumn, red berries; thorny low-care hedge at 3 per m.
Dark glossy leaves on red stalks; scented white spires in June; clips into hedges and standards.
Low, wide laurel for shady underplanting and slopes; white candles in spring; leaves toxic.
Backbone of native hedgerows at 3–5 per m; May blossom, red haws for birds; very thorny.
White blossom on bare twigs; sloes for gin after the first frost; suckers freely, long thorns.
Native hedgerow dogwood; wine-red autumn leaves, black berries for birds; suckers freely.
Pink capsules with orange seeds and crimson autumn leaves; good in mixed hedges; all parts poisonous.
The farmyard Holunder: flowers for cordial in June; berries are edible only when cooked.
Finely cut near-black leaves and pink flower plates; cut back hard in spring for best foliage.
White lacecaps, glossy red berries and red autumn leaves; copes with wet soil; raw berries toxic.
Bauerngarten classic: sterile lime-to-white snowballs, no berries; watch for aphids and leaf beetle.

origin: C & S Europe, N Africa, W Asia
notes: Chalk-loving native with felted leaves; berries turn red then black; tough on dry, limy sites.
Thorny native for wildlife hedges; food plant of the brimstone butterfly; berries are purgative.
Thornless native for damp soil; bees visit all summer; brimstone food plant; berries poisonous.
Tough native for shady mixed hedges; creamy paired flowers; red berries are mildly poisonous.
Silver leaves; vitamin-rich orange berries on females (needs a male nearby); thorny and suckering.
Scented purple-pink flowers on bare twigs in late winter; resents moving; all parts very toxic.
Dense, shade-tolerant native hedging currant at 3 per m; leafs out very early; clips well.
The Bauernjasmin: orange-blossom scent in early June; thin out old stems after flowering.
Compact mound smothered in white starry flowers in May; good low informal hedge.
Ruby-red trumpets in May–June, a few later; cut out a third of old stems after flowering.
Arching wands covered in white clusters in May; prune straight after flowering; very tough.
Flat carmine-pink heads all summer; cut back hard in early spring; tough low hedge.
Arching stems smothered in pink, yellow-throated bells; peeling bark; thin old wood after bloom.
Butterfly magnet; cut back hard in March; self-seeds invasively, so deadhead or pick sterile kinds.
Violet-blue mallows with a red eye from July; leafs out very late (May), so don't give up on it.
Lime-green cones ageing white then pink; flowers on new wood, so cut back hard in March.
Huge white snowballs on new wood; cut to 20 cm in spring; heads may flop after heavy rain.
Oak-shaped leaves turn burgundy in autumn; white cones in July on old wood, so prune lightly.
Clusters of sweetly scented pink flowers on bare twigs from November to March, paused by hard frost.
Layered horizontal tiers of white lacecaps in May; burgundy autumn leaves; needs no pruning.
Evergreen winter bloomer: pink buds open white Nov–Apr, then metallic blue berries; good hedge.
Scarlet, gold-centred flowers on thorny twigs in early spring; small quinces make fragrant jelly.
Double golden pompons in April–May; bright green stems in winter; spreads by suckers.
Arching mound covered in pure white flowers in April–May; prune lightly after flowering.
Dark evergreen smothered in deep blue puffs in May; short-lived (10–15 yrs); best on a warm wall.
Glossy aromatic evergreen; scented white flowers in May, often again in autumn.
Male form: red buds all winter open to scented white flowers in spring; needs acid soil and shade.
Scarlet young shoots fade pink then green; white bell flowers in spring; needs acid soil, shelter.
Glossy evergreen with early spring blooms; acid soil; avoid morning sun on frosted buds.
Honeysuckle-scented yellow flowers in May, fiery autumn colour; needs acid soil; toxic.
Compact evergreen azalea smothered in clear pink in spring; needs lime-free, humus-rich soil.
Starry, lightly scented white flowers in March before the leaves; late frost can brown them.
Spidery scented yellow flowers on bare branches Feb–Mar; slow; orange-yellow autumn colour.
Coral-red stems all winter; cut out a third of old stems each March for the best colour.
Tiered large shrub with white star bracts in June, strawberry-like edible fruits, red autumn.
Weeping mound of lacy purple-red leaves turning orange-red; shelter from wind and scorching sun.
Deep purple leaves, pinkish-white domes in June, peeling bark; very hardy and easy.
Late-summer haze of blue loved by bees; aromatic grey leaves; cut back to 15 cm each spring.
Syn. Potentilla fruticosa: big yellow flowers June–October; very hardy; low hedge or border.
Holly-leaved evergreen for shade; yellow spring flowers, blue-black berries; bronze in winter.
Gold-speckled evergreen for deep, dry shade and city gardens; red berries only on female plants.
Bold glossy hand-shaped leaves for shade; cream flower balls in autumn feed late insects.
Semi-evergreen with lightly scented pinkish-white bells July–October; much loved by bees.
Golden saucers July–September; semi-evergreen; cut back by a third in spring; copes with part shade.
Marble-white berries into winter (toxic); suckering and tough for shade, slopes and poor soil.
Herringbone branches for walls and banks; bees love the flowers; red berries and autumn leaves.
Arching semi-evergreen with sage-green leaves and orange-red berries; informal hedges and screens.
Thorny evergreen for walls and intruder-proof hedges; white May flowers, orange berries all winter.
Compact lilac with scented pink-lilac panicles in May, often a few more in late summer; mildew-resistant.
Classic double white Lemoine lilac from Nancy; richly scented; remove spent heads and suckers.
Large rich-yellow flowers before the leaves; prune right after flowering, removing old stems.
Gold-edged evergreen for low edging and groundcover; pink-tinged in winter; may climb walls.
Rich pink rosettes with the quintessential Old Rose scent; can be trained as a short climber.
Velvety deep crimson cups with strong Old Rose scent; compact and bushy for the border front.
Soft pink cupped rosettes with fruity scent; exceptionally healthy; among the first to flower.
Rich pure yellow cups with a tea scent; tall and arching, can be trained as a short climber.

common: Rambling rose 'The Lady of the Lake'
notes: Rare repeat-flowering rambler: sprays of semi-double soft pink with a citrus scent; to about 4 m.
Rich salmon-coral rosettes with myrrh-tinged scent; upright, healthy and good for cutting.
Clusters of deep pink, almost magenta blooms; very healthy; light tea scent.
Medieval Red Rose of Lancaster; semi-double crimson, once-flowering in June; suckers into thickets.
Crimson-and-white striped sport of the Apothecary's rose; once-flowering; good low hedge.
Velvety violet-purple pompons, once in June; nearly thornless; thin out after flowering.
Pure white Damask with a green button eye, raised at the Luxembourg Gardens; superb scent.
Rose des Peintres of Dutch flower paintings: heavy, globular pink blooms; once-flowering.
Tough, tall Alba with grey-green leaves and creamy double flowers; tolerates some shade.
Bourbon with cupped, camellia-like warm pink blooms and rich scent; repeats well.
Huge quartered magenta blooms, among the most fragrant of all roses; can be trained as a climber.
Compact Portland with quartered clear pink blooms and strong scent; repeats; fits small gardens.
White floribunda sold as Schneewittchen in Germany; flowers non-stop until frost; can get blackspot.
Bred as 'Madame A. Meilland', Gloria Dei in Germany: huge yellow blooms edged pink; light scent.
Classic velvety dark red hybrid tea; healthy, long-stemmed and long-lasting in the vase.
Healthy, reliable repeat-flowering climber with silvery-pink scented blooms; copes with north walls.
Vigorous once-flowering rambler: coppery buds open to scented salmon-pink blooms; mildew-prone.
Rampant rambler for trees and sheds: huge sprays of small scented white flowers, then red hips.
Very vigorous rambler for big trees: cascading sprays of small blush-pink, musk-scented flowers.
Old-fashioned cream cups blushed carmine; healthy repeat climber for arches; only light scent.
Noisette climber with blush-white scented blooms over a long season; reliable on north walls.
Old buff-apricot Tea-Noisette climber with rich tea scent; best on a warm wall; early and long.
Native hedgerow rose: pale pink flowers in June, red hips for jam and tea; arching and thorny.
Salt-proof hedge rose; scented magenta flowers all summer, big edible hips; invasive on dunes.
Grey-purple foliage, small cerise-pink single flowers and red hips; native to the Alps and Pyrenees.
Low suckering native of dunes and heaths; creamy flowers in May–June, black hips; tough cover.
Apple-scented leaves, strongest after rain; single pink flowers and red hips; thorny hedgerow rose.
Group 1: smothered in vanilla-scented pink flowers in May; prune only straight after flowering.
Group 2: mauve-pink with carmine bars in May–June and again in September; fades in full sun.
Group 3: velvety deep purple flowers July–September; cut back to 30 cm in late winter.
Group 3 Viticella: masses of dark violet nodding flowers; wilt-resistant; cut back hard in February.
Group 1 evergreen with almond-scented white flowers in March–April; needs a warm, sheltered wall.
Scented lilac racemes in May before the leaves; prune in July and February; needs a very strong support.
Long racemes open from the base as the leaves unfold; ideal for pergolas; prune July and February.
Native woodbine; evening-scented flowers for moths, red berries for birds; keep roots shaded.
The German Jelängerjelieber: cupped leaves around very fragrant cream-pink flowers in May–June.
Self-clinging evergreen for walls or shady groundcover; its autumn flowers are vital for late insects.
Five-fingered leaves turn brilliant crimson; climbs by tendrils with sticky pads; keep out of gutters.
Self-clinging with adhesive pads, clothes whole façades; glowing scarlet autumn colour.

origin: S & C Europe to W Asia (cultivated)
notes: Train on a pergola or warm wall; prune hard in winter; table grapes ripen September–October.
Herbaceous twiner reaching 6 m each summer, dying back in winter; papery green cones on females.
Orange trumpets July–September on a hot wall; clings with aerial roots; spur-prune; suckers.
Intensely scented white flowers all summer; twiner for warm walls and arches; thin after flowering.
Glossy evergreen with heavily scented white star flowers; red-tinted in winter; to about −10 °C.
Self-clinging climber for north walls; white lacecaps in June; slow for 2–3 years, then vigorous.
Semi-evergreen twiner with chocolate-purple, spicy vanilla-scented flowers in April; vigorous.
Needs one male per 6–8 females (or self-fertile 'Jenny'); strong pergola; shoots are late-frost tender.

origin: Japan, Korea, China, Russian Far East
notes: Grape-sized smooth kiwis eaten skin and all; very hardy; plant a male for every few females.
'Mile-a-minute': grows 4–6 m a year and smothers all; only to hide big eyesores; foamy white flowers.
Exotic white-and-blue flowers all summer, then orange fruits; semi-evergreen; regrows after frost.
Magenta bracts spring to autumn on hot walls; frost-tender, so overwinter indoors north of the Alps.
